The Fairlight CMI is a digital synthesiser, sampler and digital audio workstation launched by Fairlight of Australia in 1979; it is a keyboard / electrophone / mechanical hybrid, H-S number 412/31/52. It contains a keyboard, a processing box, a graphic display, an interactive light pen, a standard keyboard, analogue-to-digital conversion hardware and an eight-inch disk; you play it by triggering samples from the keyboard and shaping the attack, sustain, decay and vibrato. On 1980s pop recordings it was used by musicians such as Peter Gabriel, Kate Bush and Stevie Wonder.
起源於1975年，Kim Ryrie與Peter Vogel在澳洲雪梨成立Fai: It began in 1975, when Kim Ryrie and Peter Vogel founded Fairlight in Sydney, Australia, and later licensed the Qasar M8 developed by Tony Furse. In 1978 the two replaced conventional synthesis with recorded samples, and in 1979 they brought out the Fairlight CMI. In 1982 the Series II added the Page R sequencer, which simplified arranging and made the instrument more widespread. Through the use of musicians such as Peter Gabriel, the CMI reached recording studios in Britain and the USA and became an important tool of 1980s pop production.
